title: Longest feature film you’ve seen in one sitting

commenti.body:
It would really help if you could edit your original post to tell us all how long those movies were without us having to Google their duration.

A couple of months ago I finally saw in the cinema a screening of the master Edward Yang’s A Brighter Summer Day (1991). 

It clocked in at 237 minutes/4 hours long with zero breaks. While it was the longest movie I’ve ever watched it didn’t drag at all.

I know it is in Sight and Sounds top 100 of all time along with my favourite Yang movie Yi Yi (2000). If a director has two films in the top 100 you know they are worth watching.
Good idea, add them to the post!

*Killers of the Flower Moon*, actually. Hadn't been to a theater in quite a while, but had to go for Marty. I think very long movies are great, but I think you need an intermission in case nature is calling, and even just to give your brain a break so you can focus on the rest of the film better. Of course at home, you can make your own intermission.

Museum of Fine Art Houston had a screening of Matthew Barney's Remaster Cycle one time. All 5 films in one day, with a break for lunch. One of the 5 films was over 3 hours long. Altogether the cycle is over 7 hours I believe. Would fucking love to see them all again like that.

I wonder more about the experience of watching such long movies and if you felt it was worth the time and patience. 

I personally think the longest in one sitting has been A Brighter Summer Day which was absolutely magnificent in the second viewing. In three sittings was Satantango, which stays as an intriguing and mysterious, at times nihilistic film in my own memory.

Probably either *Lawrence of Arabia* (3:47) or *The Godfather, Part II* (3:22). I definitely watched the latter in one sitting, but I’m not sure  about *Lawrence*.

I don’t have that kind of stamina any more, especially as so few movies over 2 hrs actually justify their runtimes. For every *A Brighter Summer’s Day* or *An Elephant Standing Still* there a dozen “Spectre”s or *Dial of Destiny”.

I usually do my research before endeavoring, movies with a slow-burning, meditative flavor require a different kind of mental effort in comparison to informative, or story-based ones, which require higher levels of concentration. The first kind usually focuses on the mood, whereas the second and third focus on a linear succession of events. For example, I would say that the temporal experience watching Bernardo Bertolucci's 1900 is vastly different than that of Chantal Akerman's Jeannne Dielman. Based on that I usually decide if I want to watch a movie in one sitting. In general it feels slow and heavy in the beginning, but once I get into it, I start to experience a temporal flow.  

The example named in this post by Lav Diaz is extremely slow and requires low-levels of sustained concentration spread on a longer span, like running a marathon. Most directors who decide to take this choice of making the movie excruciatingly long have the intention to engage their audience in a sort of a meditative state: an invoked boredom. Even if it is not the best movie ever, I would say that it is worth the 10-hours if you are interested in the substance. I think any avid movie lover should experience that kind of movies at least once. It is not like I would watch a Lav Diaz every week haha, maybe once every decade or two.

Happy hour (2015) is a Japanese movie I forgot to mention. It chronicles the decay and falling apart of a friendship between four women. I felt it. I did not just watch it. Yup. Experienced it. It is a next level cinema.
